title: Why a Week of Tech Failures Felt Like One Big Attack
summary:
When a string of tech failures hit in the same week, many people online wondered: could they all be connected? Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase, and U.S. Bank had technical problems and outages that delayed flights and interrupted workdays. Marriott and Apple customers had digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a November 16 cyberattack. At the same time, several U.S. government systems, including the Federal Aviation Administration, ran into trouble.

The pileup felt suspicious to many people. "We're under attack in a way we've never seen before," wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer, on November 17. "This is an AI cyberattack." "Coincidence???" wrote Christopher Webb, a self-described "lifelong Dem" and party strategist, on November 16. But the best available information points to ordinary explanations, such as routine maintenance or one-off problems, rather than a coordinated attack.

So why is that hard to believe? Psychologists say part of the answer is how our brains work. "Detecting patterns is important for perceiving the world and learning about cause and effect," said Javier Granados Samayoa, a Texas Christian University psychology professor. But that habit, he said, "can sometimes lead people to see connections where none may exist." One study linked pattern-spotting in random coin tosses to believing conspiracy theories. Research also shows that when people feel they lack control, they are more likely to spot patterns that are not really there.

"People are looking for ways to understand what is going on and they don't like the uncertainty that often surrounds unfolding events," said Karen Douglas, a social psychology professor at the University of Kent. "Also, a simple explanation is often not very appealing." On social media, negative posts tend to spread further. Axios reported that an estimated 30% of the most alarming posts came from suspected bots.
why_it_matters: When scary stories spread fast online, knowing how our brains look for patterns can help us pause, check the facts, and avoid being fooled by rumors.

keywords.explanation: An outage is a time when a service or system stops working.
An influencer is a person with many followers online whose posts can shape what others think.
A conspiracy theory is a belief that a secret group is behind an event, without good proof.
Bots are computer programs that act like people online, for example by posting messages.
Maintenance is routine work done to keep something running well.
